notes.meaning: Moses places the choice pieces of meat and the special breads directly onto the hands of Aaron and his sons. They wave these gifts back and forth before the Lord as an act of presentation. Filling their hands with these offerings marked the formal beginning of their work as priests.

Moses takes the waved offerings back from their hands and burns them on the altar over the regular burnt offering. Because the new priests were not yet fully consecrated, Moses acted as the officiating priest on God's behalf. Burning the food completely showed total surrender to God and created a pleasing aroma before Him.

Moses takes the breast of the ordination ram and waves it before the Lord as a wave offering. Because Moses carried out the duties of the priest during these ceremonies, this portion belonged to him as food. This established the rule for later peace offerings, where the officiating priest received the breast.

God commands that the breast and the right thigh of the ordination ram be set apart as holy portions. The breast was waved back and forth, and the thigh was lifted up before the Lord. Both portions were reserved for Aaron and his sons to establish their future priestly rights.

These portions were to be given to Aaron and his family as a permanent rule whenever the people offered peace offerings. Peace offerings were shared meals that celebrated fellowship and thanksgiving toward God. Providing this meat ensured that the priests were fed while they served the community before the Lord.

Aaron's sacred garments were not to be discarded after his death, but passed down to his descendants. Future high priests would wear these same holy clothes when they were anointed and ordained into office. This tradition showed the continuous and lasting nature of the high priestly calling.

The son who succeeded Aaron as high priest had to wear these sacred clothes for seven full days before ministering in the Holy Place. Seven represents completion in Scripture and gave the incoming priest time to reflect deeply on his heavy responsibilities. This ensured that every new high priest entered his holy duties with great reverence.

Moses takes the remaining meat of the ordination ram and boils it in a holy place. This boiling was done inside the courtyard of the Tabernacle near the entrance. Preparing the food in this holy setting readying it for a sacred meal in God's presence.

Aaron and his sons ate the boiled meat and the remaining basket bread right at the doorway of the Tent of Meeting. Eating a meal at God's door showed joyful friendship and peace between the Lord and His newly appointed priests. It pictured God welcoming them as close companions at His table.

The priests ate the food used in the sacrifices that made atonement for them. Atonement means their sins were covered and cleansed so they could safely stand before a holy God. No outsider was allowed to eat this meal, because these foods were completely set apart for the priests.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars translate atonement as wiping clean or erasing sin, rather than the traditional picture of covering it over.

notes.meaning: Any meat or bread left over until the following morning had to be burned completely with fire. Because the food was sacred, it could not be allowed to spoil or be eaten as ordinary leftovers. This rule protected holy things from being treated in a careless or common way.

Moses was instructed to repeat these ordination ceremonies every day for seven full days. Carrying out the ritual over a full week gave Aaron and his sons time for calm thought and spiritual preparation. It also ensured that a Sabbath day passed over them before they took up their duties.

Each day of the seven days, Moses sacrificed a young bull as a sin offering to make atonement. The altar itself had to be cleansed with blood and anointed with oil to set it apart for God. Even the altar needed purification because human hands had built it and sinful people would serve around it.

After seven days of cleansing, the altar became most holy. Anything touching the altar belonged entirely to God and was treated as holy. Christian teachers see the altar as a picture of Christ, who makes our prayers and spiritual gifts pleasing to God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this verse as reflecting an ancient concept where holiness acted like a physical charge that spread by touch, placing anyone who touched the altar in danger of death.

notes.meaning: God commands the priests to offer two one-year-old lambs on the altar every single day without interruption. This daily offering showed Israel's constant need for forgiveness and regular dedication to the Lord. It reminded the nation of God's continuous care and pointed ahead to the lasting work of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the instructions for the daily offerings were added here later from Numbers 28, noting that early Israel may have offered only a morning burnt offering.

notes.meaning: One lamb was offered early in the morning, and the other lamb was offered at twilight. These two sacrifices marked the beginning and the end of each day with worship. They teach believers to start and finish every day by offering prayers and thanks to God.

Along with the morning lamb, the priest offered fine flour mixed with olive oil and a drink offering of wine. The flour and oil amounted to about three quarts, while the wine was about one quart. Presenting bread and wine alongside the lamb recognized that all daily food and drink come from God's hand.

The second lamb offered at twilight received the very same grain and drink offerings as the morning sacrifice. It was burned completely on the altar as a pleasing aroma before the Lord. This demonstrated that God desires the same faithful devotion at the close of the day as at the start.

This daily burnt offering was to continue down through the generations at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The name Tent of Meeting shows that this was the place where God chose to speak with His people. God met them at the altar, showing that true fellowship with Him depends on sacrifice.

The Lord promised that He would meet with the whole assembly of Israel at the sanctuary. The place was made holy not by human effort alone, but by the glorious presence of God Himself. When God revealed His glory there, the entire camp was set apart as His own.

God promises to personally consecrate the Tent of Meeting, the altar, and Aaron with his sons. Moses performed the ceremonies, but only God's personal blessing could truly make people and objects fit for holy service. True ministry begins when God Himself calls and equips His servants.

The Lord promised that He would live directly in the midst of Israel and be their God. The Tabernacle served as the palace of their divine King right in the middle of the camp. His dwelling there gave the people constant comfort, guidance, and protection.

By living among them, God proved to the people that He was the same Lord who brought them out of Egypt. The ultimate goal of the Exodus was not just freedom from slavery, but fellowship with God in their daily lives. Having the Lord dwell with them was the greatest gift of their rescue.
